Life Science · Grades 5 to 7

The Pump and the River of Blood

Your body is a living city. Every cell needs deliveries, and every cell makes trash. Meet the network that never stops working: your heart, your blood, and your vessels.

An interactive lesson on the circulatory system
Scroll to begin
Part One

A city that never sleeps

Imagine your body as a huge city. Every house needs food, water, and oxygen. Every house also makes garbage that must be hauled away. The job of running these deliveries and pickups belongs to one system.

The circulatory system, also called the cardiovascular system, is the delivery-and-pickup network that keeps your body alive. It has three main parts working together.

Three parts, one team: a pump, a road network, and a moving river
The real network inside a body: the heart at the center, with arteries branching out everywhere.

The word cardiovascular comes from two parts: cardio, meaning heart, and vascular, meaning vessels. So the cardiovascular system is simply the heart-and-vessel system.

■ Stop and think

If your body is a city, which part of the circulatory system is most like a fleet of delivery trucks? Which part is most like the roads they drive on?

Part Two

Why blood must keep moving

Your cells are alive. They need oxygen and nutrients to make energy, and they produce carbon dioxide and waste. Blood acts like a moving supply chain that never takes a day off. It carries many different cargoes at once.

  • 🚚
    Oxygen from the lungs to body cells
  • 🍲
    Nutrients from digested food to cells
  • ♻
    Carbon dioxide from cells back to the lungs
  • 🗑
    Waste to organs that remove it
  • ✉
    Hormones that carry chemical messages
  • 🛡
    Immune cells that fight infection

Blood is not just red liquid. It is living tissue made of liquid and solid parts. The liquid part is called plasma, and the solid parts include red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets. Over half of all your blood is plasma.

Cells crave oxygen, an element whose atom carries eight electrons. Blood is the courier that delivers it.
Part Three

The heart: two pumps in one

The heart sits near the center of your chest, tilted slightly to the left. We call it a pump, but it is more accurate to say it is two pumps working side by side. One side pushes blood to the lungs. The other side pushes blood to the rest of the body.

Right side to the lungs. Left side to life.
Left: a real heart with its great vessels. Right: the pulmonary circuit, the loop that runs between the heart and the lungs.

Two great loops

Blood travels through two major circuits. The pulmonary circuit runs from the heart to the lungs and back. There, blood drops off carbon dioxide and picks up fresh oxygen, like an empty truck reloading at a supply station.

The systemic circuit runs from the heart to the whole body and back. Oxygen-rich blood delivers its cargo to cells, then oxygen-poor blood returns to start the trip again.

▶ Quick check
Which circuit sends blood to the lungs to pick up oxygen?
Part Four

Four rooms inside the heart

The heart is divided into four chambers, or rooms. The two upper rooms are called atria. The two lower rooms are called ventricles. Blood flows into the atria, drops down into the ventricles, and the ventricles pump it out.

Upper rooms receive. Lower rooms pump.
Two views of the four chambers. The arrows on the left show which way blood moves through each room.

Look closely at the bottom left of the diagram. The left ventricle has the thickest, strongest muscle wall of all four chambers. That is because it must push blood all the way around the body. The right ventricle only has to send blood to the nearby lungs, so it does not need to be as strong.

■ Stop and think

Why would the chamber that pumps blood to your toes need a thicker muscle than the chamber that pumps blood to your lungs right next door?

Part Five

Follow one drop of blood

Blood does not wander randomly. It follows a fixed path, a loop it travels again and again. Watch a single drop make the full journey.

The drop turns from blue to red as it picks up oxygen in the lungs
Oxygen-rich blood (red) enters from the lungs and heads out to the body. Oxygen-poor blood (blue) returns and heads to the lungs.

The eight steps

1. Oxygen-poor blood returns from the body to the right atrium. 2. It drops into the right ventricle. 3. The right ventricle pumps it through the pulmonary artery to the lungs. 4. In the lungs, blood releases carbon dioxide and grabs oxygen.

5. Oxygen-rich blood returns to the left atrium. 6. It drops into the left ventricle. 7. The left ventricle pumps it into the aorta. 8. The aorta sends oxygen-rich blood out to the whole body, and the loop begins again.

▶ Quick check
A drop of blood just left the lungs full of oxygen. Where does it go next?
Part Six

One-way doors

Blood must move in the correct direction. It cannot slosh backward every time the heart squeezes. That is the job of the valves. A valve is like a one-way door. It swings open to let blood pass forward, then snaps shut so blood cannot leak back.

When doctors hear "lub-dub," that sound is mostly valves snapping shut
A real aortic valve opening and closing. A healthy valve (left pair) opens wide; a stiff one (right pair) cannot.

The heart has four main valves. They sit between the chambers and at the exits, making sure every drop moves one way only.

ValveWhere it sitsJob
TricuspidRight atrium to right ventricleKeeps blood moving down on the right
PulmonaryRight ventricle to pulmonary arteryControls the flow toward the lungs
MitralLeft atrium to left ventricleKeeps blood moving down on the left
AorticLeft ventricle to aortaControls the flow toward the body
Part Seven

The river system

Blood travels inside tubes called blood vessels. There are three main kinds, and they branch from huge to tiny like the limbs of a tree.

Big artery → tiny capillaries → back through the vein
Left: an artery branches into a web of capillaries, then merges into a vein. Right: red blood cells crowding through a vessel.

Arteries

An artery carries blood away from the heart. Most arteries carry oxygen-rich blood, but there is one famous exception: the pulmonary artery carries oxygen-poor blood toward the lungs. Arteries have thick, elastic walls because blood is pushed through them under high pressure.

Veins

A vein carries blood back to the heart. Most veins carry oxygen-poor blood, but the pulmonary veins are the exception, carrying oxygen-rich blood from the lungs. Veins have thinner walls and often contain small valves to keep blood from flowing backward.

Capillaries

A capillary is the tiniest vessel of all, so narrow that blood cells move through it in single file. This is where the real magic happens. Oxygen and nutrients slip out of the blood into your cells, and carbon dioxide and waste slip in to be carried away.

▶ Quick check
Where do oxygen and nutrients actually move from blood into your body's cells?
Part Eight

What blood is made of

Scoop up a drop of blood and you would find a busy mixture: a liquid river crowded with tiny cells, each with its own job.

Cells floating in plasma, which is more than half of all your blood
A real look at the mixture: red blood cells, a white blood cell, and platelets all riding in the yellowish plasma.

Plasma is the liquid river water, mostly water plus salts, proteins, nutrients, and waste. Red blood cells are the oxygen trucks. They carry a protein called hemoglobin that grabs oxygen in the lungs and hands it to cells.

White blood cells are the security guards, defending against germs. And platelets are the repair crew, rushing to patch a cut so you stop bleeding.

Part Nine

Partners: the heart and lungs

The heart and lungs are a team. Your lungs load blood with oxygen. Your heart moves that loaded blood wherever it needs to go. Watch the exchange happen inside a tiny air sac.

Blood passes the air sac, drops off carbon dioxide, and picks up oxygen
The trade inside an air sac, or alveolus: oxygen moves into the blood while carbon dioxide moves out.

So breathing and blood flow are linked. You breathe in air, oxygen enters tiny air sacs, blood flowing past picks it up, and the heart pumps that oxygen-rich blood out to every cell. Cells make carbon dioxide, blood carries it back, and you breathe it out.

Part Ten

One beat, one squeeze, one relax

A heartbeat is one complete squeeze-and-relax cycle. It is not random. The heart has its own electrical control system that keeps a steady rhythm. Each beat has two phases.

Systole is the squeeze, when the heart muscle contracts and pushes blood out. Diastole is the relax, when the chambers fill again with blood, ready for the next beat.

Squeeze, relax, fill, repeat, about 60 to 100 times a minute at rest
Finding your pulse at the wrist, just below the thumb. Each beat you feel is one push of blood.

Your pulse

Your pulse is the beat you can feel in an artery each time the heart pushes blood through it. You can find it on your wrist below the thumb, on the side of your neck, or inside your elbow. When you exercise, your muscles cry out for more oxygen, so your heart beats faster and your pulse speeds up.

Blood pressure

Blood pressure is the force of blood pushing against artery walls. A reading like 110 over 70 has two numbers: the higher one is the squeeze pressure, the lower one is the relax pressure. The big idea is simple: blood does not just drift. It is pushed, and that push creates pressure.

▶ Quick check
During systole, the heart muscle is doing what?
Part Eleven

Sorting truth from myth

Blood looks red because red blood cells carry hemoglobin, which contains iron and binds oxygen. Oxygen-rich blood is bright red. Oxygen-poor blood is darker red, but it is still red. Human blood is never blue inside your body. Veins look bluish only because of the way light passes through skin.

Bright red oxygen-rich blood on the left, darker oxygen-poor blood on the right. Both are red, never blue.
Veins are blue because the blood inside is blue.
Blood is always red. Veins just look blue through the skin because of light and tissue.
All arteries carry oxygen-rich blood.
Usually, but not always. The pulmonary artery carries oxygen-poor blood to the lungs.
All veins carry oxygen-poor blood.
Usually, but not always. The pulmonary veins carry oxygen-rich blood from the lungs.
The heart is shaped like a Valentine heart.
A real heart is more like a muscular fist or a cone of living muscle.
Blood just floats around the body.
Blood is pushed by the heart through a closed system of vessels.
Real hearts are muscular cones, nothing like a Valentine. A cut-open heart, a 3D model, and a preserved human heart.
■ Stop and think

Every analogy has limits. We call the heart a pump and blood a river. Where does that comparison work well, and where does it break down?

Part Twelve

Exercise and a stronger heart

When you run, dance, or jump rope, your muscles work harder and demand more oxygen and fuel. Your heart answers by beating faster and stronger. Over time, regular activity strengthens the heart muscle itself, the same way lifting strengthens any other muscle.

ActivityWhat happens to the heart
Walking fastHeart rate rises a little
RunningHeart rate rises a lot
Jump ropeHeart and lungs work hard together
SwimmingHeart pumps more blood to muscles
DancingHeart speeds up to supply the muscles

Health guidelines suggest kids and teens get at least 60 minutes of moderate-to-vigorous activity every day. Most of it should be aerobic, the kind that makes your heart beat faster. Healthy habits help too: a balanced diet, plenty of water, enough sleep, and steering clear of smoking and vaping all protect your heart for the long haul.

A real heart-rate trace: the pulse climbs once exercise starts, peaks, then eases back down during recovery.
